repos.name: JustVugg / colibri
repos.description: Run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own — pure C, zero deps, experts streamed from disk. Tiny engine, immense model. 🐦

summary.goal: Colibrì is a pure-C inference engine designed to run frontier Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models ranging from 744B to 2.8T parameters on consumer and heterogeneous hardware. It treats storage, RAM, and VRAM as a single inference memory hierarchy, and is described as both a usable engine and an open research platform for inference-side performance work.
summary.usage: Users can download a prebuilt release or build from source with `git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri && cd colibri/c` followed by `./setup.sh`. After obtaining a converted model (e.g., a ~372GB GLM-5.2 container from Hugging Face), the engine is run with commands such as `./coli chat`, `./coli serve`, or `./coli web`.
summary.pros: Nine model families (including GLM-5.2, Kimi K3, and OLMoE) share the same `coli chat`/`coli serve`/`coli web` front end, and none of the supported models requires a GPU. A learning cache records routing history so the engine becomes faster the more it is used, and an optional dual-SSD setup can increase aggregate read bandwidth for streaming experts.
summary.cons: Model weights are large -- the reference GLM-5.2 container is about 372GB, and other families range up to roughly 1.6TB for Kimi K3, so a sizeable, ideally fast, disk appears to be a prerequisite. The README also states there is no SLA on inference speed, only a guarantee on model semantics, so performance may vary with available fast memory and drive characteristics such as O_DIRECT support.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited to users who already own consumer or heterogeneous hardware (CPU, optional GPU, and adequate disk) and want to run very large MoE models locally rather than through a hosted API. It may also suit those interested in contributing to or experimenting with inference-systems research, given its stated role as an open research platform.

repos.name: bilawalsidhu / gods-eye-view
repos.description: A spy satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real. Live open source spatial intelligence on a photorealistic 3D globe.

summary.goal: God's Eye View is a browser-based, photorealistic 3D globe that visualizes live public data streams, including aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic, and public cameras, alongside a voice-controlled AI agent for hands-free navigation.
summary.usage: Install via Pinokio (8.2 or later) with one click, or run locally: `git clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git`, `cd gods-eye-view`, `npm ci`, `npm run doctor`, `npm run dev`, then open `http://localhost:4173`. Node.js 24.14.0+ or 26.x is required.
summary.pros: Most layers, including flights, ships, satellites, earthquakes, and public cameras, work without any API keys. Sensitive credentials are brokered through a server-side proxy rather than exposed to the browser, and the project is released under the MIT License.
summary.cons: Photorealistic 3D rendering requires a free Cesium ion token or a metered Google Maps key, both subject to provider quotas and terms; Node.js 25 is explicitly unsupported (flagged as end-of-life by the setup doctor), and voice features depend on a metered OpenAI key with associated per-minute costs.
summary.fit: Based on the README's framing, this project appears best suited for developers, hobbyists, and researchers exploring geospatial visualization and public data feeds; it does not appear intended for safety-critical or production deployments, as the README explicitly warns against use for navigation, emergency response, medical, or investment purposes.

repos.name: tech-leads-club / agent-skills
repos.description: The secure, validated skill registry for professional AI coding agents. Extend Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and more with absolute confidence.

summary.goal: Agent Skills is an npm-distributed registry of curated, security-reviewed skills — packaged instructions and resources — that extend AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and others with new workflows and specialized knowledge.
summary.usage: Skills are installed by running `npx @tech-leads-club/agent-skills`, which launches an interactive wizard for choosing skills, target agents, install method (copy or symlink), and scope. Direct CLI commands are also available, e.g. `agent-skills install -s tlc-spec-driven`, alongside list, update, remove, cache, and audit subcommands; skills can also be served to MCP-compatible clients via the `@tech-leads-club/agent-skills-mcp` server.
summary.pros: Every skill is scanned with Snyk Agent Scan before publishing, the CLI applies defense-in-depth measures (sanitization, path isolation, symlink guards, atomic lockfile, audit trail), the codebase is stated to be 100% open source with CI static analysis, and it supports a wide range of Tier 1-3 agents including Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.
summary.cons: Node.js >=22 is required, and using the skills catalog requires mandatory attribution to Tech Leads Club regardless of context; third-party skills retain separate licenses that need individual checking.
summary.fit: Given its broad multi-agent support and stated security tooling, it may suit teams or developers already using agents like Claude Code or Cursor who want a centrally managed, vetted source of reusable skills rather than an open marketplace.

repos.name: calesthio / OpenMontage
repos.description: World's first open-source, agentic video production system. 12 production pipelines, 100+ tools, 700+ agent skill and production-knowledge files. Turn your AI coding assistant into a full video production studio.

summary.goal: OpenMontage is described as an open-source, agentic video production system that turns an AI coding assistant into a video production studio, handling research, scripting, asset generation, editing, and final composition from plain-language descriptions.

The README also notes that local LLM support via Ollama/LM Studio is only 'coming soon,' suggesting a cloud-based AI assistant is presently required.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited to developers who already use one of the supported AI coding assistants and want to generate short videos (explainers, documentaries, trailers, social clips) through natural-language prompts rather than manual editing tools.

repos.name: multimodal-art-projection / YuE
repos.description: YuE2: frontier music generation with symbolic planning, zero-shot covers, and agentic music editing.

summary.goal: YuE2 is a music generation system that unifies symbolic (melody-and-chord) planning with audio synthesis, turning lyrics and a style prompt into a complete song with vocals and accompaniment, while also supporting zero-shot covers and agentic editing of compositions.
summary.usage: Installation follows `git clone https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/YuE.git`, `cd YuE`, and `python -m pip install .` inside a Python 3.12 virtual environment; a first song can then be produced with `python examples/generate.py --output outputs/first-song`. The staged Python API exposes plan(), generate_semantic(), synthesize(), and decode() via the YuE2Pipeline class, with model weights such as m-a-p/YuE2-3B downloaded from Hugging Face on first use.
summary.pros: YuE2 is reported to be competitive with Suno v5/v6 on the WildSongBench benchmark, with a best-of-8 setting achieving 6.9632 SongBench Avg, described as the highest observed mean among evaluated settings. Its symbolic planning stage makes melody and chords explicit and editable before audio rendering, and the same checkpoint reportedly supports zero-shot covers and agentic editing.
summary.cons: Running YuE2 requires a Linux system with an NVIDIA GPU supporting BF16 and 24 GB VRAM, which may limit accessibility on lower-end or non-Linux hardware. The documentation also notes that the small gap between top benchmark scores does not establish statistical significance, so any performance edge may not be fully conclusive.
summary.fit: YuE2 appears suited for developers and researchers who have GPU-backed infrastructure and want an inspectable, editable composition stage rather than a purely end-to-end black-box generator for music-generation or AI-agent workflows.

repos.name: alphaXiv / OpenResearch
repos.description: Turn your coding agents into research agents

summary.usage: Install with `curl -LsSf https://openresearch.sh/install.sh | sh` and run `orx up`, which opens a local dashboard at `http://127.0.0.1:4791`; remote GPU sessions start with `orx up --remote user@host`, and `orx install-skills` installs the OpenResearch skill into supported agents.

summary.fit: Based on the README, it appears suited to developers and researchers who want to run research or coding agents locally or on remote compute while keeping code and experiment data locally owned; official release builds also send opt-out, coarse usage telemetry tied to a random installation ID unless disabled.

repos.name: debpalash / VoiceStudio

An interactive `./install.sh` script also supports targeted or category-specific installs, and individual SKILL.md files can be piped into Claude Code or pasted into Claude.ai project prompts.

repos.name: alibaba / open-code-review
repos.description: Fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

summary.goal: Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool that reads Git diffs and sends changed files to a configurable LLM through an agent with tool-use capabilities, producing structured, line-level review comments. `ocr scan` additionally reviews whole files for auditing codebases without a meaningful diff.
summary.usage: Requires Git >= 2.41. Install with `npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`, then configure a provider and model with `ocr config provider` and `ocr config model` (unless using Delegation Mode), and run reviews with commands such as `ocr review` or `ocr scan`.

Its 'deterministic engineering + agent' design is presented as addressing incomplete coverage, position drift, and unstable quality issues attributed to purely language-driven agents.
summary.cons: The benchmark shows lower Recall than general-purpose agents, described as a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise, which suggests some real defects may be missed. Running the default mode requires configuring an LLM, though Delegation Mode avoids this step.
summary.fit: The tool appears suited for teams wanting precision-focused code review integrated with CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.) across Windows, macOS, and Linux, with integrations for coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

repos.name: jihe520 / MathModelAgent

repos.name: tonhowtf / omniget

repos.name: huggingface / transformers
repos.description: 🤗 Transformers: the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning models in text, vision, audio, and multimodal models, for both inference and training.

summary.goal: Transformers acts as a model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning across text, vision, audio, video, and multimodal tasks, supporting both inference and training, and centralizing model definitions so they work across the broader ecosystem of training and inference frameworks.
summary.usage: After installing Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.5+, install the library with `pip install "transformers[torch]"`. Use the high-level `Pipeline` API (e.g. `pipeline(task="text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B")`) for inference, or chat with a model from the command line via `transformers chat Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`.

summary.fit: This makes it a good fit for developers and researchers who want ready-to-use, state-of-the-art models across modalities, but it may be less suited for teams needing a fully customizable neural-network building-block toolbox or generic (non-PyTorch-centric) training loops, and included example scripts may need adaptation to specific use cases.

repos.name: ayghri / i-have-adhd
repos.description: A skill to stop your coding agent from burying the answer. ADHD-friendly output.

summary.goal: i-have-adhd is a skill/plugin for coding assistants designed to prevent responses from burying the answer, prioritizing an action-first format with numbered steps and no closing pleasantries such as "Hope this helps!"
summary.usage: Installation is done by copying a CLI prompt that references https://github.com/ayghri/i-have-adhd and the repository's AGENTS.md file, or by following INSTALL.md. To customize it, users fork the repo, edit skills/i-have-adhd/SKILL.md, then run commands such as `claude plugin marketplace add <your-username>/i-have-adhd` and `claude plugin install i-have-adhd@i-have-adhd`, restart Claude Code, and re-invoke `/i-have-adhd`.

summary.cons: Customizing the skill requires forking the repository and manually running uninstall/marketplace-remove/add/install commands, since the fork and upstream share the same plugin name. The README also notes the approach is adapted for how an LLM should respond, not for how a person should organize their day, suggesting it may not function as a general ADHD management tool despite its name.
summary.fit: The plugin appears best suited for developers using AI coding assistants such as Claude Code who want concise, action-first responses rather than exploratory or hedged explanations; it does not appear intended as a clinical or personal ADHD support tool.

repos.name: affaan-m / ECC
repos.description: The agent harness performance optimization system. Skills, instincts, memory, security, and research-first development for Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, Cursor and beyond.

summary.goal: ECC is an MIT-licensed open-source "agent harness operating system" that adds a structured engineering workflow (plan, test, implement, review, verify, remember, improve) on top of AI coding agents. It ships 68 agents, 292 skills, and 94 legacy command shims, plus hooks, rules, memory, and AgentShield security scanning, and works primarily with Claude Code.
summary.usage: The recommended install runs `npx ecc-universal@2.2.1 setup` for guided Claude Code plugin setup, or natively inside Claude Code via `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` followed by `/plugin install ecc@ecc`. Only one install method should be used per harness to avoid duplicated skills, commands, or hooks.
summary.pros: ECC bundles a large, pre-built catalog (68 agents, 292 skills) covering planning, TDD, code review, build repair, security, and domain-specific workflows, so teams do not need to assemble this tooling from scratch. It also includes AgentShield scanning for prompts, hooks, MCP configs, and secrets, and supports self-hosted or custom model endpoints without changing ECC's workflows.
summary.cons: The README states ECC "works best with Claude Code today" and that adapters for other harnesses (Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Zed, Copilot, and others) are "capability-limited," so full feature parity across harnesses is not guaranteed and should be checked before assuming equivalent behavior. Setup also requires Node.js 18+, and Claude plugin setup additionally requires Git and Claude Code 2.1+.
summary.fit: ECC appears best suited for teams already standardized on Claude Code who want a structured, tool-assisted development workflow with reusable skills and security scanning. Teams relying primarily on other harnesses may get a reduced feature set, since the documented platform support table lists several integrations as beta, experimental, or instruction-only rather than at full parity.

repos.name: openai / plugins
repos.description: OpenAI Plugins

summary.goal: This repository provides a curated collection of example plugins for Codex, demonstrating how developers can build plugin bundles for tools such as Figma, Notion, SwiftUI-based iOS/macOS apps, web apps, Expo, Netlify, Remotion, and Google Slides.
summary.usage: Each plugin is organized under plugins/<name>/ and must include a .codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest, with optional companion files like skills/, .app.json, .mcp.json, agents/, commands/, hooks.json, and assets/. The default marketplace configuration is located at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json, pointing to the plugins/ directory.
summary.pros: The repository offers several richer, real-world examples spanning design (Figma), knowledge work (Notion), mobile/desktop development (build-ios-apps, build-macos-apps, expo), and web deployment (build-web-apps, netlify), giving developers multiple reference implementations for learning plugin structure.
summary.cons: Users authenticating with an API key appear to rely on a separate marketplace file (.agents/plugins/api_marketplace.json) rather than the default one, which suggests the plugin discovery setup may differ depending on login method and could require additional configuration awareness.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for developers already working within the Codex ecosystem who want reference examples for building or extending plugins across design, productivity, and app-development domains, rather than for those seeking a single standalone tool.

repos.name: mksglu / context-mode
repos.description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and   enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks.

summary.goal: Context Mode is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server built for AI coding agents. Its documented goal is reducing how much raw tool output — such as file reads, web fetches, and command results — enters the model's context window, while also preserving session state such as edited files and pending tasks across conversation compaction.
summary.usage: Claude Code users install it as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode` followed by `/plugin install context-mode@context-mode`, then restart Claude Code and run the diagnostics command to confirm the install. The documented prerequisite for this plugin path is Claude Code v1.0.33+; other supported clients register the same server as an MCP tool provider instead.
summary.pros: The README states that raw command output is processed inside an isolated sandbox subprocess, so only relevant results reach the conversation, with one documented example of a 315 KB session output reduced to about 5.4 KB — roughly a 98% reduction. It also documents no telemetry and no required account, since session data stays local.
summary.cons: On platforms without hook support, such as the Antigravity IDE and Zed, the README states that routing enforcement depends on a manually copied instruction file rather than automatic interception, and estimates this reaches only about 60% of the context savings achieved with hooks. The Cursor plugin is also documented as still awaiting marketplace review.
summary.fit: Based on the company logos presented as users, Context Mode appears suited to both individual developers and engineering teams working across MCP-compatible AI coding clients — the README documents support for 17 such clients plus an OpenClaw gateway integration. It is released under the Elastic License 2.0, a source-available license disallowing hosted or managed-service offerings.

repos.name: DietrichGebert / ponytail
repos.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.

summary.goal: Ponytail is a rule-set/plugin for AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex that guides them toward minimal, non-over-engineered code. Before writing new code, it follows a priority ladder — skip unneeded code (YAGNI), reuse existing code, use the standard library, native platform features, or an installed dependency, or write one line — while never cutting validation, error handling, security, or accessibility.
summary.usage: Installation is host-specific; for Claude Code it requires two separate prompts: `/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail` followed by `/plugin install ponytail@ponytail`. Other hosts, such as Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI, have their own install commands. Slash commands like `/ponytail` and `/ponytail-review` switch between lite, full, ultra, and off intensity levels; a `PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE` environment variable can set the default (full by default).
summary.pros: Benchmarks against a no-skill baseline, run on a real FastAPI + React repo using Claude Code with Haiku 4.5, report ponytail cutting lines of code by 54%, cost by 20%, and time by 27%, while keeping 100% safety — better than a bare 'YAGNI + one-liners' prompt, which dropped to 95% safety.
summary.cons: The Claude Code and Codex plugins rely on two Node.js lifecycle hooks, so `node` must be on PATH or always-on activation stays silent instead of erroring. The headline benchmark numbers come from a small sample (n=4) on one model (Haiku 4.5) and one repo, so the measured gains may not generalize to other codebases or models.
summary.fit: The project reportedly works with 20 agent hosts per its badge, including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, and OpenCode. The `/ponytail` slash commands need a 'skill-capable host'; instruction-only adapters like Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot Chat, Kiro, and Antigravity load the always-on ruleset but without the commands.

repos.name: tt-a1i / archify
repos.description: Agent skill for beautiful, verifiable architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, and lifecycle diagrams—self-contained HTML with motion and crisp export.

summary.goal: Archify is a Node.js rendering and validation system for AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode) that turns a codebase or system description into an interactive system map directly in chat. Agents produce typed JSON IR that Archify deterministically compiles into HTML/SVG diagrams.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npx skills add tt-a1i/archify -g`, then describe a system in an agent chat (no repository required) or ask the agent to analyze a repository and generate an architecture diagram. The CLI also offers commands such as `node archify/bin/archify.mjs guide "Show an API request with Redis cache miss"` for choosing a diagram type.
summary.pros: Output passes atomic checks (schema, layout, HTML/SVG, routing) before delivery, and interactions like tracing reach or routes reuse only authored data rather than inventing topology. Results are portable as a single self-contained HTML file, with optional PNG, SVG, WebM, and share-card exports, plus an Architecture Delta mode that compares Before/After snapshots for review.
summary.cons: Archify explicitly excludes automatic Mermaid parsing, general-purpose auto-layout, hosted sharing, and WYSIWYG editing, positioning it as neither a general drawing editor nor a Mermaid theme. Some features, such as the deployment-ownership profile, fail closed and require explicitly authored data (owners, region, database scope) rather than inspecting live infrastructure.
summary.fit: Archify appears suited to developers using supported agent CLIs/IDEs (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, and via ZIP, Claude.ai or Raven) who want agent-generated architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, or lifecycle diagrams for documentation or pre-merge review, rather than teams needing a general-purpose interactive diagram editor.

repos.name: openai / skills
repos.description: Skills Catalog for Codex

summary.goal: This repository catalogs Agent Skills — folders of instructions, scripts, and resources — for use and distribution with the Codex AI agent platform. Skills package capabilities so teams and individuals can complete tasks in a repeatable way.
summary.usage: Skills in the `.system` folder install automatically in the latest Codex. Curated or experimental skills are installed via the `$skill-installer` command inside Codex, e.g. `$skill-installer gh-address-comments`, or by specifying a GitHub directory URL: `$skill-installer install https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.experimental/create-plan`. Codex must be restarted afterward for the skill to take effect.
summary.pros: Skills are reusable across projects ('write once, use everywhere') and installable with simple named commands through `$skill-installer`. System skills need no manual setup, and the Agent Skills format follows an open standard rather than a proprietary one.
summary.cons: The repository is explicitly marked deprecated, with current Codex skill and plugin examples redirected to the openai/plugins repository, so future updates or support for skills here appear uncertain. A Codex restart is also required after each install.
summary.fit: This repository likely suits existing Codex users wanting prepackaged, repeatable skills, though given the deprecation notice, those seeking current examples would probably be better served by openai/plugins instead. Licensing is defined per skill in its own LICENSE.txt file.

repos.name: heygen-com / hyperframes
repos.description: Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

summary.goal: HyperFrames is an open-source (Apache 2.0) framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos, usable locally through a CLI, through AI coding agent skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.
summary.usage: Agents typically install the core skill set with `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`, while manual use starts a project with `npx hyperframes init my-video`, then previews and renders it with `npx hyperframes preview` and `npx hyperframes render` to produce an MP4 locally.
summary.pros: HyperFrames compositions are authored as plain HTML with data attributes rather than React, rendering is deterministic so identical input yields the same output, the CLI is non-interactive by default for agent workflows, and the project ships 20 packaged skills plus a components catalog covering common needs like captions, charts, and transitions.
summary.cons: Running HyperFrames locally requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg as prerequisites, and cloning the full repository for development additionally requires Git LFS, since the golden regression-test baselines add roughly 240 MB of .mp4 files that must be fetched separately.
summary.fit: Based on its HTML-first, agent-friendly design and deterministic rendering, HyperFrames seems best suited to developers and AI agents automating CI or pipeline video generation, whereas teams already committed to Remotion's React-based authoring model may find switching authoring paradigms less straightforward.

repos.name: microsoft / markitdown
repos.description: Python tool for converting files and office documents to Markdown.

summary.goal: MarkItDown is a lightweight Python utility for converting files such as PDF, PowerPoint, Word, Excel, images, audio, HTML, CSV/JSON/XML, ZIP archives, YouTube URLs, and EPubs into Markdown, intended for use with LLMs and related text analysis pipelines.
summary.usage: Install with `pip install 'markitdown[all]'` and convert a file from the command line using `markitdown path-to-file.pdf > document.md`. A Python API is also documented via `from markitdown import MarkItDown`, along with optional Azure Document Intelligence or Content Understanding endpoint configuration for cloud-based conversion.
summary.pros: The documentation describes support for many file formats, optional dependency groups (e.g. `[pdf]`, `[docx]`, `[pptx]`) for installing only what's needed, and support for 3rd-party plugins such as `markitdown-ocr` that extend functionality without modifying the core repository.
summary.cons: The README's Security Considerations section states that MarkItDown performs I/O with the privileges of the current process, similar to `open()` or `requests.get()`, and advises sanitizing inputs and calling narrower `convert_*` functions in untrusted environments, implying that unrestricted use with untrusted input could carry risk.
summary.fit: The project is documented as a Python library meant to be incorporated into other systems rather than an end-user application; the contribution scope explicitly excludes web servers, REST/HTTP APIs, hosted conversion services, and desktop/mobile applications, suggesting it fits backend or pipeline integration better than standalone deployment.

repos.name: obra / superpowers
repos.description: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works.

summary.goal: Superpowers is described as a complete software development methodology for coding agents, built on composable skills paired with initial instructions that ensure the agent invokes them automatically.
summary.usage: Installation of Superpowers is harness-specific; for Claude Code, run `/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official` from the official marketplace, or register a separate marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace` followed by `/plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace`. Once installed, skills like brainstorming, writing-plans, and test-driven-development activate automatically to guide design, planning, and RED-GREEN-REFACTOR implementation.
summary.pros: The skills library covers testing, debugging, collaboration, and meta workflows, and the documented basic workflow emphasizes test-first development, code review between tasks, and evidence-based verification before completion. It supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI, among other supported harnesses.
summary.cons: Because installation differs by harness, using Superpowers with more than one coding agent requires installing it separately for each, which could add setup and update overhead.
summary.fit: This methodology appears best suited to teams already working with one of the supported coding agents who want a structured, mandatory design-to-implementation workflow, and may be less fitting for those seeking a lightweight, optional process.

repos.name: coreyhaines31 / marketingskills
repos.description: Marketing skills for Claude Code and AI agents. CRO, copywriting, SEO, analytics, and growth engineering.

summary.goal: This repository offers a collection of AI agent skills for marketing tasks—conversion optimization, copywriting, SEO, analytics, and growth engineering. It targets technical marketers and founders using AI coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, or Windsurf, and works with agents that support its skill format. Built by Corey Haines, it is MIT-licensed.
summary.usage: Skills install via `npx skills add coreyhaines31/marketingskills`, or through Claude Code's plugin system using `/plugin marketplace add coreyhaines31/marketingskills` followed by `/plugin install marketing-skills`. Once installed, users ask their agent for marketing help or invoke a skill directly, such as `/cro`.
summary.pros: The collection organizes 50 skills across categories like conversion optimization, copy, SEO, paid distribution, and retention. A `product-marketing` skill serves as a shared foundation other skills reportedly check first, suggesting the skills form an interconnected system rather than standalone scripts. It is free and MIT-licensed.
summary.cons: Upgrading from v1.x to v2.0 requires manually deleting stale old-named skill folders, since 17 skills were renamed and `page-cro` (plus `form-cro`) merged into `cro`, and the installer adds new skills alongside old ones instead of replacing them. Moving an existing product marketing context file to its new location and filename is also a manual step, though old paths reportedly still work as a fallback.
summary.fit: The skills suit technical marketers and founders using AI coding agents for marketing execution; a companion guide targets those newer to terminals and coding agents. Because installation steps focus mainly on Claude Code and a shared universal directory, support depth for other listed agents may vary in the documentation.

repos.name: ChromeDevTools / chrome-devtools-mcp
repos.description: Chrome DevTools for coding agents

summary.goal: chrome-devtools-mcp (Chrome DevTools for agents) is a Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server that lets coding agents such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor, or Copilot control and inspect a live Chrome browser, with a CLI also provided for use without MCP.
summary.usage: An MCP client is configured to run `npx -y chrome-devtools-mcp@latest` to start the chrome-devtools-mcp server; for basic browser tasks only, the `--slim` and `--headless` flags can be added. A first test prompt asking to check the performance of a URL confirms the browser opens and records a trace.
summary.pros: chrome-devtools-mcp uses Chrome DevTools to record traces and extract performance insights, supports advanced browser debugging such as analyzing network requests, screenshots, and source-mapped console messages, and relies on Puppeteer for reliable automation that automatically waits for action results.
summary.cons: Using chrome-devtools-mcp requires Node.js LTS, a current stable version of Chrome, and npm installed beforehand, and it officially supports only Google Chrome and Chrome for Testing, so other Chromium-based browsers may show unexpected behavior.
summary.fit: chrome-devtools-mcp appears suited for developers building agentic tooling who want an integrated browser subagent for automation, debugging, and performance analysis, though by default it collects usage statistics and can send trace URLs to Google's CrUX API unless disabled with flags.

repos.name: cathrynlavery / diagram-design
repos.description: 38 editorial diagram types for Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Self-contained HTML + SVG. No shadows. No Mermaid slop.

summary.goal: Diagram Design is an Agent Skill that generates 39 editorial-style diagram types (architecture, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and more) as self-contained HTML and SVG for Claude Code, Codex, Factory Droid, Pi, and other Agent Skills-compatible hosts. It appears to target developers and writers who want on-brand, non-generic diagrams without relying on Figma or default AI-generated styling.
summary.usage: Install via `/plugin marketplace add cathrynlavery/diagram-design` followed by `/plugin install diagram-design@diagram-design` in Claude Code (similar commands exist for Codex, GitHub Copilot, Factory Droid, and Pi). After installing, users can open `skills/diagram-design/assets/index.html` to browse all 39 diagrams, or ask the agent in natural language to produce a specific diagram type.
summary.pros: Diagrams ship as a single self-contained HTML file with no build step, JavaScript, or external image dependency. Accessibility is built in by default (ARIA roles, resolving accessible names, WCAG AA contrast checks), and the skill can also redraw existing draw.io, Mermaid, or Excalidraw sources while producing a fidelity ledger of what changed.
summary.cons: PNG export requires a one-time separate setup step (`pip install playwright && playwright install chromium`), which adds an external dependency beyond the core skill install. Auto-update for third-party marketplaces is also disabled by default in Claude Code, requiring a manual toggle to keep the plugin current.
summary.fit: Documented use cases where this skill is not recommended include quick unicode diagrams for tweets or terminals, plain lists, before/after comparisons, and single-box diagrams, suggesting it fits multi-node, structured diagrams rather than simple content. It seems best suited for teams that want diagrams matching their website's brand colors and fonts through the onboarding flow.

repos.name: THU-MAIC / OpenMAIC
repos.description: Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom — Get an immersive, multi-agent learning experience in just one click

summary.goal: OpenMAIC (Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom) is an open-source AI platform that turns a topic or document into an interactive classroom, generating slides, quizzes, simulations, and project-based learning activities delivered by AI teachers and classmates. Released August 27, 2026, v1.0.0 adds a chat-based Pro workbench that plans, builds, and revises whole courses alongside the original one-click generator.
summary.usage: To run locally, clone the repo with `git clone https://github.com/THU-MAIC/OpenMAIC.git` and run `pnpm install`. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and set at least one LLM provider API key. Start it with `pnpm dev` and open http://localhost:3000. Node.js >= 22.19 and pnpm >= 10 are required; Docker and Vercel deployment are also documented.
summary.pros: It combines slides, quizzes, interactive HTML simulations, and PBL activities with real-time multi-agent discussion, whiteboard drawing, and text-to-speech. Lessons export as editable .pptx or self-contained HTML, and offline exports inline external assets for air-gapped playback. The interface supports 12 locales, and an OpenMAIC Skill lets it be triggered from agent workbenches like OpenClaw, Codex, DeepSeek, or WorkBuddy.
summary.cons: Using OpenMAIC requires configuring at least one LLM provider API key, since none is bundled by default. Optional features like MP4 video export, local FunASR speech recognition, or MinerU parsing each need separate services or extra setup rather than working out of the box.
summary.fit: Based on its use-case examples — generating lessons on programming, game rules, or research papers — OpenMAIC seems best suited to individual learners, educators, and developers wanting to self-host or extend an AI-driven course-authoring platform, rather than users seeking a fully managed, zero-configuration service.

repos.name: Tencent / WeKnora
repos.description: Open-source LLM knowledge platform: turn raw documents into a queryable RAG, an autonomous reasoning agent, and a self-maintaining Wiki.

summary.goal: WeKnora is an open-source, LLM-powered knowledge framework (version 0.8.0) built for enterprise-grade document understanding, semantic retrieval, and autonomous reasoning. It combines RAG-based Quick Q&A, a ReAct Agent that orchestrates retrieval and tools, and a Wiki Mode that turns raw documents into an interlinked, self-maintaining markdown knowledge base.
summary.usage: Set up by running `git clone https://github.com/Tencent/WeKnora.git`, then `cd WeKnora` and `docker compose up -d` to start core services (Docker, Docker Compose, and Git are listed prerequisites). The Web UI is then reachable at `http://localhost`. Optional Docker Compose profiles such as `neo4j`, `minio`, and `langfuse` can enable additional components.
summary.pros: The README documents support for 20+ LLM providers (including OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Ollama), 10+ document formats, multiple vector databases and object-storage backends, and several IM channel integrations. It is released under the MIT License and describes a fully modular, self-hostable architecture where LLMs, vector stores, and storage can be swapped.
summary.cons: The project's Security Notice advises deploying WeKnora within an internal or private network rather than exposing it directly to the public internet, implying that additional hardening (firewalls, access controls) beyond the built-in login authentication added since v0.1.3 is expected for production use.
summary.fit: Given its stated emphasis on local or private-cloud deployment and full data sovereignty, WeKnora seems best suited for organizations seeking a self-hosted, enterprise document Q&A and knowledge-base platform rather than a ready-made managed cloud service.

repos.name: blader / humanizer
repos.description: Agent skill that removes signs of AI-generated writing from text

summary.goal: Humanizer is a Markdown-based skill that rewrites AI-sounding text so it reads as if written by a person, without changing what the text says. According to the README, it works with any agent that supports skills.
summary.usage: Install it with the Skills CLI using `npx skills add blader/humanizer --global` for a global install, or omit `--global` for a project-only install; the skill responds to `/humanizer`. On Claude Code 2.1.142 or newer, it can instead be installed as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer` and `/plugin install humanizer@humanizer`, responding to `/humanizer:humanizer`. Claude Desktop requires a manual install by downloading the repo as a ZIP or copying SKILL.md into the agent's skill folder.
summary.pros: The rewrite process shows its work: an initial draft, a short critique, and a final version. It edits only prose, leaving code, data, frontmatter, and link targets unchanged, and the README states it does not invent facts, asking for missing details instead. It also supports voice matching from a writing sample, and organizes its checks into 25 numbered patterns ordered by strength and frequency.
summary.cons: Several patterns are documented as 'weak alone,' meaning they justify an edit only when multiple tells appear together in a passage, since a careful writer may use any one deliberately; this suggests some rewrite decisions may need human judgment in ambiguous cases.
summary.fit: This tool appears suited to users of skill-supporting agents such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop who want a documented, pattern-based way to reduce AI-sounding phrasing while preserving factual content; the README does not indicate support for agents lacking skills capability.

repos.name: max-sixty / worktrunk
repos.description: Worktrunk is a CLI for Git worktree management, designed for parallel AI agent workflows

summary.goal: Worktrunk is a command-line tool for managing git worktrees, built for running multiple AI coding agents (such as Claude Code and Codex) in parallel. It provides three core commands intended to make working with worktrees as straightforward as working with branches.
summary.usage: Worktrunk can be installed via Homebrew with `brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install`, or via Cargo with `cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install` (Windows, Arch Linux, and Conda/Pixi installs are also documented). A typical workflow starts a worktree with `wt switch --create feature-auth`, then inspects worktrees with `wt list`.
summary.pros: The README documents features such as hooks for automating setup at various workflow stages, LLM-generated commit messages, a merge workflow that squashes and rebases in one command, an interactive picker with diff/log previews, shared build caches across worktrees, and PR checkout support.
summary.cons: Shell integration must be explicitly installed via `wt config shell install` for commands to change directories, and on Windows the `wt` command name conflicts with Windows Terminal's own command, requiring installation as `git-wt` instead unless that alias is disabled.
summary.fit: Worktrunk appears best suited for developers who run several AI coding agents in parallel using git worktrees and want a CLI to reduce the manual steps git worktree normally requires; it documents support for macOS, Linux, Windows, and Arch Linux.

summary.goal: skills is a collection of Claude Code skills published by HumanLayer (https://humanlayer.dev), distributed for installation into a project.
summary.usage: Skills are installed with `npx skills add humanlayer/skills --skill SKILLNAME`, substituting SKILLNAME with a listed skill name such as improve-claude-md, narrow-react-prop-types, build-iterated-agentic-loop, design-control-loop, or show-me; each is then invoked in the project with its own slash command, for example `/improve-claude-md` or `/show-me`.
summary.pros: The repository offers five distinct skills: tuning CLAUDE.md instruction adherence, narrowing React prop types to live code paths, scaffolding an iterated coding-agent GitHub Actions workflow, interactively designing an agentic control loop, and producing concise explanatory diagrams or HTML artifacts.
summary.cons: Installing skills requires a Node.js environment capable of running `npx skills add humanlayer/skills --skill SKILLNAME`; the README does not describe alternative installation methods or indicate compatibility with non-npm workflows.
summary.fit: This project appears suited for developers already using Claude Code who want ready-made, narrowly scoped skills for documentation tuning, React typing, agentic workflow scaffolding, or visual explanations, rather than a general-purpose standalone tool.

repos.name: earthtojake / text-to-cad
repos.description: A library of agent skills for CAD, CAE and CAM

summary.goal: text-to-cad is a library of agent skills for CAD, CAE, and CAM work, covering generating, inspecting, sourcing, slicing, and handing off CAD and robot-description artifacts from local project files.
summary.usage: Install with the Skills CLI via `npx skills add earthtojake/text-to-cad`, the documented preferred path; provider-native plugin installs are also available for Codex, Claude Code (`claude plugin install cad@text-to-cad`), and Grok Build.
summary.pros: The library bundles skills spanning CAD generation with STEP/STL/3MF/GLB export, a step.parts finder for off-the-shelf parts, DXF drawing creation, URDF/SRDF/SDF robot-description authoring, G-code slicing, and Bambu Labs print handling, released under the MIT license.
summary.cons: Running `npx skills update` only refreshes skills already present in the lockfile and silently misses skills added in newer releases, so keeping the full skill set current relies on rerunning `npx skills add` instead.
summary.fit: This appears best suited to agent-driven CAD/robotics workflows within supported agent environments such as Codex, Claude Code, and Grok Build, though not every supported agent is explicitly enumerated.

repos.name: petergyang / no-ai-slop
repos.description: Removes 20+ patterns of AI slop from any piece of writing.

summary.goal: No AI Slop is a skill for removing more than 20 documented patterns of "AI slop" writing—such as binary contrasts ("It's not X. It's Y."), throat-clearing openers, and fake-profound endings—while aiming to preserve the writer's personal voice.
summary.usage: Install it by pasting "Install the /no-ai-slop skill globally from https://github.com/petergyang/no-ai-slop" into ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent, or by running npx skills add petergyang/no-ai-slop --skill no-ai-slop --global --yes. Then invoke /no-ai-slop (your writing) to edit text, or /no-ai-slop is this slop? (your writing) to detect slop patterns.
summary.pros: The README states the editing mode preserves personal voice and lists what it changed, while the detection mode quotes every slop pattern found. It also checks writing fundamentals such as leading with the point, active voice, and concrete detail over abstraction.
summary.cons: The detection mode explicitly quotes slop patterns "without guessing whether AI wrote the text," so it likely cannot confirm authorship, only flag matching phrasing patterns.
summary.fit: Given its install path, it appears best suited to people already working inside ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or similar coding-agent environments to review or generate writing.

repos.name: github / spec-kit
repos.description: 💫 Toolkit to help you get started with Spec-Driven Development

summary.goal: Spec Kit is an open source toolkit for Spec-Driven Development (SDD), a workflow where specifications are written and refined before implementation and then used to generate working code with any AI coding agent.
summary.usage: Install with `uv tool install specify-cli --from git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@vX.Y.Z`, then run `specify init my-project --integration copilot` and `cd my-project` to scaffold a project. From there, agents run slash commands such as /speckit.constitution, /speckit.specify, /speckit.plan, /speckit.tasks, and /speckit.implement to move from principles to a completed feature.
summary.pros: Spec Kit bundles two optional, opt-in workflows beyond the core SDD flow: bug fixing (assess → fix → test) and idea assessment (intake → research → define → shape → decide). It also integrates with 30+ AI coding agents, both CLI tools and IDE-based assistants.
summary.cons: Using Spec Kit requires several prerequisites: uv (or pipx for persistent installs), Python 3.11+, Git, and a supported AI coding agent, so setup is not a single self-contained step. Community-created extensions, presets, and bundles are maintained independently of the core project.
summary.fit: Given its structured, multi-phase workflow spanning greenfield development, creative exploration, and iterative/brownfield enhancement, Spec Kit appears best suited to teams and organizations that already use AI coding agents and want a repeatable, documented process for translating specifications into implementations.

repos.name: kunchenguid / firstmate
repos.description: Talk to one agent. Ship with a crew.

summary.goal: firstmate is documented as an agent distro for running a crew of AI coding agents. Instead of operating one agent directly, users chat with a single 'first mate' that spawns and supervises autonomous 'crewmate' agents, each working in an isolated git worktree, returning finished pull requests, approved local merges, or investigation reports.
summary.usage: Setup starts with `git clone https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate`, `cd firstmate`, and GitHub authentication via `gh auth login`. A supported primary harness such as Claude Code is then launched (e.g. `claude`), which reads `AGENTS.md` and instantiates the first mate; tasks are given via natural-language chat and return PR links or reports.
summary.pros: Each task runs in its own disposable git worktree so parallel work never collides, and every crewmate's session is visible in its own tmux window or equivalent backend tab that a user can watch or type into. Supervision is described as event-driven and zero-token, and state persists on disk so the fleet can recover after a session is killed.
summary.cons: Because firstmate has no separate installer and functions as the cloned repository itself, some harnesses likely require trusting and pre-approving project-level hooks. For instance, Grok needs a one-time `--trust` flag per clone, and Pi requires approving a one-time trust prompt per clone before its hooks auto-load.
summary.fit: Given its reliance on a verified primary agent harness, Git, and the GitHub CLI, firstmate appears best suited to developers already using tools like Claude Code, Grok, or Pi who want to coordinate multiple parallel coding tasks across isolated worktrees rather than run a single agent session.

repos.name: omacom / omarchy
repos.description: Beautiful, Modern & Opinionated Linux

summary.goal: Omarchy is presented as a Linux distribution created by DHH, described as "beautiful, fun & agentic," with more information available at https://omarchy.org.
summary.usage: Its documentation is organized in a manual/ directory, also mirrored at https://learn.omacom.io/2/the-omarchy-manual, covering topics such as Getting Started, Hotkeys, and the Omarchy CLI; since no separate installation command is given, setup and navigation appear to begin with the "Getting Started" and "Coming From Mac or Windows" manual pages.
summary.pros: It is released under the MIT License (https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT), and its manual spans roughly fifty pages covering applications, configuration, theming, hardware, security, and troubleshooting topics.
summary.cons: Because documentation is split across dozens of separate manual files rather than one consolidated guide, users may need to check multiple pages to piece together full setup or configuration details, and cross-platform users may need to rely on the separate "Windows VM" and "Mac support" pages, suggesting native support is Linux-centric.
summary.fit: Omarchy appears best suited to Linux users wanting a preconfigured desktop environment with built-in AI, development, and theming tools, though platform or hardware prerequisites beyond the listed manual topics are not specified.

repos.name: anthropics / claude-plugins-community
repos.description: Community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. Read-only mirror — submit plugins at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission.

summary.goal: Claude Plugins — Community is documented as a read-only mirror of the community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. The .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file lists plugins available for installation, synced nightly from Anthropic's internal review pipeline.
summary.usage: Plugins can be installed from claude.com/plugins/ for Claude Cowork, or through the Claude Code CLI, which requires first adding the marketplace and then installing a specific plugin by running `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community` followed by `claude plugin install <plugin-name>@claude-community`.
summary.pros: Every listed plugin has passed automated security scanning and been approved for distribution before appearing in the marketplace. Submissions go through a single, centralized intake point at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission rather than ad hoc channels.
summary.cons: Because the marketplace list syncs only nightly from an internal pipeline, the visible plugin set may lag behind the actual review state by up to a day; exact update timing and discrepancy handling are not detailed in the source material.
summary.fit: This repository appears suited for users who want to browse and install pre-vetted plugins through the documented web interface or CLI, rather than contribute code directly, since pull requests opened against the repo are closed automatically.

repos.name: AprilNEA / OpenLogi
repos.description: ⚡️A native, local-first alternative to Logitech Options+, written in Rust 🦀 — remap buttons, DPI, and SmartShift over HID++. No account, no telemetry.

summary.goal: OpenLogi is a native, local-first alternative to Logitech Options+, written in Rust, that unlocks additional capabilities of Logitech mice, keyboards, and webcams over the HID++ and UVC protocols. It runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows and is currently under active development, so features and configuration may still change.
summary.usage: Before installing, quit Logi Options+, since the two applications cannot share HID++ access to the same receiver. On macOS 13 or later, install via Homebrew with `brew install --cask openlogi`. Linux users can instead install a `.deb` package from the latest GitHub release (https://github.com/AprilNEA/OpenLogi/releases/latest) using `sudo dpkg -i openlogi-*.deb`.
summary.pros: OpenLogi keeps a light native Rust/GPUI footprint, treats Linux as a first-class platform, and stores all settings in one syncable TOML file. It supports assigning gesture roles to any physical button, per-application profile overlays, and a scriptable CLI alongside the GUI. Device-specific controls include DPI presets, SmartShift wheel settings, keyboard RGB lighting, and detailed UVC webcam image adjustments.
summary.cons: The project is explicitly marked as under active development and not yet stable, meaning features and configuration format may change before a stable release. Pre-built Linux packages require GLIBC 2.35 or newer (an Ubuntu 22.04 baseline), which could limit compatibility with older Linux distributions.
summary.fit: OpenLogi may suit users who want a native, open-source, cross-platform replacement for Logitech Options+ with scriptable configuration, particularly on Linux where Options+ has no official client. It is not affiliated with Logitech, so it could be less suitable for users who need official vendor support or a fully stabilized release.

repos.name: cursor / plugins
repos.description: Cursor plugin specification and official plugins

summary.goal: This repository, cursor/plugins, is a marketplace of official Cursor plugins for developer tools, frameworks, and SaaS products. Each plugin lives in its own directory at the repository root containing a `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, with a root `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json` listing all plugins.
summary.usage: Each plugin directory includes its own `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest along with `skills/`, `rules/`, `mcp.json`, `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and `LICENSE` files; the root `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json` aggregates all plugin listings for the Cursor marketplace.
summary.pros: The collection spans over sixty plugins across categories such as Developer Tools, Productivity, and Integrations, covering tools like GitHub, Gmail, Google Drive, Salesforce, and Playwright, each maintained as a standalone package with its own documentation and license.
summary.cons: Because most plugins live under `third_party/` and connect to external SaaS products such as Gmail, Salesforce, and HubSpot, using them likely requires separate accounts or credentials for each connected service, a detail the README does not elaborate on.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for teams already using the Cursor editor who want to extend its agents with a broad set of developer-tool and SaaS integrations, rather than users seeking a standalone application.

repos.name: volcengine / OpenViking
repos.description: Self-evolving Context Database for AI Agents. Unify Agent Memory, Knowledge RAG and Skills.

summary.goal: OpenViking is presented as an open-source context database for AI agents, giving them a place to store knowledge, remember users, and reuse experience across sessions. It organizes this context as a virtual filesystem reachable through a viking:// URI scheme, browsable with commands such as ls, tree, read, and write.
summary.usage: Installation starts with `pip install openviking --upgrade`, then `openviking-server init` configures provider and model settings before the server is started. Users then rely on the bundled `ov` CLI to import and search resources, for example adding a GitHub repository and running semantic queries against it. It requires Python 3.10+ and access to an embedding model plus a VLM, cloud-hosted or local.
summary.pros: According to the project's benchmark report, an OpenViking 0.3.22 evaluation found three agent integrations rising from 24–57% to 80–83% accuracy on the LoCoMo memory benchmark, while input tokens dropped 34.3–91.0% and query latency dropped 58.45–66.10%. On tau2-bench, task success rose by +6.87pp (retail) and +11.87pp (airline) versus the same LLM without memory. These figures come from the specific models and setups tested and may not generalize to every configuration.
summary.cons: Running OpenViking requires Python 3.10+ plus access to both an embedding model and a VLM, cloud-hosted or local, before the server will start. The core project is released under AGPLv3, and documentation advises configuring authentication before exposing a deployed server beyond localhost.
summary.fit: The open-source server can be self-hosted under AGPLv3 with no activation key, suiting teams building agent integrations that need persistent, cross-session memory. Organizations wanting managed hosting or distributed production deployments can instead choose the Managed SaaS or license-key-based Self-Managed (BYOC) commercial editions; the companion desktop console remains in beta for macOS and Windows x64.

repos.name: freestylefly / awesome-gpt-image-2
repos.description: Prompt as Code | GPT Image 2 / 2.5 提示词与案例库，530+ 个案例、20+ 套工业级模板与可复用 Skills，新增 2.5 同提示词对比专区，附完整提示词与生成记录，持续更新。

summary.goal: awesome-gpt-image-2 is a prompt-engineering repository built around GPT-Image2, offering an "industrial prompt engine" and template library. It documents 544 reverse-engineered cases plus reusable templates, aiming to turn prose-style prompts into structured, composable protocols for batch and automation-friendly image generation, including a GPT Image 2.5 spotlight section.
summary.usage: Users can browse the case gallery and templates directly on GitHub, or explore the companion site at https://gpt-image2.canghe.ai. To add the bundled Agent Skill, run `npx skills add freestylefly/awesome-gpt-image-2 --skill gpt-image-2-style-library --agent claude-code codex --global --yes --copy`, or inside Claude Code run `/plugin marketplace add freestylefly/awesome-gpt-image-2`.
summary.pros: The repository organizes 544 cases into clear categories (UI, posters, branding, photography, and more) alongside matching prompt templates, and ships an installable Agent Skill compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, plus a visual website for side-by-side prompt comparison.
summary.cons: Enabling the companion website's paid generation and billing features requires configuring numerous Vercel environment variables (Supabase, Stripe, Google Analytics) and applying multiple Supabase SQL migrations in sequence, an operational setup that goes beyond simply browsing the static prompt library.
summary.fit: The structured, template-based approach seems best suited to users building repeatable or automated image-generation workflows with agent tools rather than one-off casual prompting, though effectiveness depends on access to the underlying GPT-Image2 model.

repos.name: vorssaint / vorssaint-utils
repos.description: Free and open-source macOS menu bar toolkit.

summary.goal: Vorssaint is a free, open-source macOS menu bar app that bundles utilities such as a volume mixer, system monitor, window manager, app switcher, clipboard history, text snippets, a file shelf, and an uninstaller into one icon, aiming to replace several separately purchased Mac apps.
summary.usage: Install with Homebrew via `brew install --cask vorssaint`, or download the disk image from the GitHub releases page (https://github.com/vorssaint/vorssaint-utils/releases) and drag Vorssaint into Applications. Individual features can be installed or removed separately from a Features page. To build from source: `git clone https://github.com/vorssaint/vorssaint-utils.git`, then run `./build.sh`.
summary.pros: The app requires no account, telemetry, or subscription; uninstalled features stop loading entirely so they use no CPU, memory, or energy; and permissions are requested only for enabled features, with each one explained and revocable in Settings.
summary.cons: It requires an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, so it likely cannot run on Intel-based Macs or earlier macOS versions. The GPL-3.0-or-later license covers only the source code, while the Vorssaint name, icon, and look are separately trademarked, meaning forks would need their own identity.
summary.fit: This tool appears best suited for Apple Silicon Mac users on macOS 14 or later who want a single, local-first, privacy-conscious app consolidating many everyday utilities; it does not appear to fit Intel Mac users or those on older macOS releases.

repos.name: modular / modular
repos.description: The Modular Platform (includes MAX & Mojo)

summary.goal: This repository hosts open-source components of the Modular Platform, described as a unified platform for AI development and deployment. It includes the MAX Framework and the Mojo Language, covering the compiler, standard library, accelerator library, inference server, and model pipelines documented in the repo.
summary.usage: Getting started with the MAX framework involves the quickstart guide at https://max.modular.com/get-started, used for serving a model. Getting started with Mojo involves the quickstart guide at https://mojolang.org/docs/manual/quickstart/. Contributions to the Mojo standard library, MAX accelerator library, or MAX model architectures should begin by reading CONTRIBUTING.md.
summary.pros: The repo lists distinct components: the Mojo compiler, Mojo standard library, MAX accelerator library, an MAX inference server with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Python-based MAX model pipelines, and code examples. It accepts community contributions to the standard library, accelerator library, model architectures, and documentation.
summary.cons: Contributions to the Mojo compiler itself are not yet accepted, so external changes there may be limited. MAX usage and distribution follow a separate Modular Community License apart from the repository's Apache License v2.0 license, which could mean users need to review third-party library licenses themselves.
summary.fit: Given its coverage of an inference server, model pipelines, and a systems language compiler, the project appears aimed at teams building and deploying AI applications who are comfortable managing multiple licenses and validating third-party dependencies themselves.

repos.name: akitaonrails / ai-memory
repos.description: Solution for long term memory for agent coding CLIs and to facilitate handoff between different agent vendors

summary.goal: ai-memory is described as long-term memory for AI coding agents, letting a session started in Claude Code continue in another agent such as OpenAI Codex in the same directory without re-explaining the architecture, failed approaches, or open questions.
summary.usage: Quick start uses Docker: run `docker run -d --name ai-memory --restart unless-stopped -p 127.0.0.1:49374:49374 -v ai-memory-data:/data docker.io/akitaonrails/ai-memory:latest` to start the server, then `ai-memory install-mcp --client claude-code --apply` and `ai-memory install-hooks --agent claude-code --apply` to wire in an agent CLI.
summary.pros: According to the documentation, its source of truth is plain markdown files in a git-backed wiki, and the default path is said to use zero LLM calls, so capture, search, and handoffs reportedly work without any API key.
summary.cons: The documented quick-start default runs with no authentication and binds only to loopback, so exposing the server on a LAN reportedly requires adding a bearer token as an extra step; native Windows support is listed as experimental rather than fully supported.
summary.fit: The project appears suited to both a single-user workstation and teams running a shared server, and setup requires Docker/Podman or, on Arch Linux, AUR packages.

summary.goal: vphone-cli boots a virtual iPhone using Apple's Virtualization.framework, built on PCC research VM infrastructure. It targets Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 15+ (Sequoia).
summary.usage: Install via Homebrew with `brew install zqxwce/tap/vphone-cli`, or build from source by cloning the repo (`git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Lakr233/vphone-cli.git`) and running the provided setup and build scripts. A virtual iPhone can then be created and started with `vphone-cli vm create myphone -V jb` followed by `vphone-cli vm launch myphone`, which downloads firmware, patches the boot chain, performs a DFU restore, and installs the chosen CFW variant.
summary.pros: The `vm create` command automates the entire pipeline from download to first boot in a single step. Five firmware variants (`less` through `exp`) offer graduated levels of security bypass, from mitigation-preserving to full jailbreak with anti-VM-detection patches. A host control socket enables programmatic screenshots, touch, and input for automated or AI-driven testing.
summary.cons: Setup requires relaxing macOS SIP and AMFI protections on the host to allow unsigned binaries with private entitlements, a change that likely reduces the host's overall security posture. The documentation also notes a known bug in the `ldid-procursus` tool (up to version 2.1.5-procursus7) that can cause the `cfw install` step to hang with unbounded memory growth, requiring a rebuild from source as a workaround.
summary.fit: The tool appears suited to developers and security researchers who need an isolated virtual iPhone environment on Apple Silicon for jailbreak research, firmware patch testing, or automated/AI-driven app testing. It is not intended for use inside a nested virtual machine host, since virtualization-based guest boot cannot nest on such configurations.

repos.name: apache / maka
repos.description: Apache Maka (Incubating) is a high-performance agent workspace that keeps a complete record of everything it did.

summary.goal: Apache Maka (Incubating) is presented as a high-performance agent workspace that keeps a complete, append-only record of everything it does, via a RuntimeEvent log capturing model messages, tool calls, and permission decisions. The README states results are benchmarked against other harnesses on the same model with an official verifier, with per-task results published in `docs/eval/`.
summary.usage: To build from source: `git clone https://github.com/apache/maka.git`, then `npm ci` and `npm run dev` to start the Desktop dev environment with HMR. Stated requirements are Node.js 22.19+ (CI uses Node.js 24), npm 11, Git, and ripgrep; Direct Peer/Peer Mesh development additionally needs Rust stable 1.98+.
summary.pros: According to the README, the RuntimeEvent log is the authoritative runtime record rather than just the UI or next prompt, sessions/settings/run records stay local while users supply their own model (cloud API, local model, or gateway), and Desktop, TUI/CLI, and Eval share a single Runtime Host execution authority.
summary.cons: The README notes Apache Maka has not made an official Apache release yet, so no signed source archive currently exists as the release artifact. It also states the project is under ASF incubation and active development, so data formats, CLI commands, and experimental capabilities may still change.
summary.fit: Based on the stated Desktop Nightly platform support (signed macOS Apple Silicon/Intel builds; unsigned Windows x64 and Linux x64/arm64 previews) and the explicit note that Nightly builds are not intended for production use, this suggests best fit for developers and testers building or evaluating agent harnesses locally.

repos.name: cordiverse / cordis
repos.description: Meta-Framework of Spatiotemporal Composability

summary.goal: Cordis (cordiverse/cordis) presents itself as 'A Meta-Framework of Spatiotemporal Composability.' Its underlying design is detailed in an accompanying paper, 'A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability' (arXiv:2608.25512), with the paper's own source hosted at https://github.com/cordiverse/paper.
summary.usage: The README does not list installation or execution commands. Current entry points are the arXiv paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25512) and a documentation page at https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/reference/cordis-primer, so hands-on usage likely depends on materials not yet fully published.
summary.pros: Having a dedicated paper describing the framework's design may help developers evaluate its architecture before adoption, and a separate paper repository (https://github.com/cordiverse/paper) suggests the underlying research is maintained independently.
summary.cons: The project is explicitly marked as under active development, and the README warns the API 'is not yet stable and may change without notice.' The official documentation is also still under construction, which may limit reliable day-to-day usage guidance for now.
summary.fit: Given the stated instability and incomplete documentation, Cordis currently appears better suited to developers tracking early-stage research or willing to accommodate breaking API changes than to teams needing a production-ready dependency.
